========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Hi, yeah, it's nice to meet you too. Um, I guess I'm here because... well, I’ve just been doing these things lately at work and at school that really just do not make any sense at all. I work as a bookkeeping clerk, right? So I deal with a lot of paperwork, mostly accounts payable, reconciling expenses, making sure the math adds up, that kind of thing. But lately, instead of just doing my job, I've been getting stuck doing this weird stuff. 

Like, the other day, I had this massive stack of expense reports, and I took all these receipts, and instead of entering them into the system, I just started lining them up across the floor. Just one by one, making this huge, perfectly straight line all the way across the office carpet, and I didn't even really know why I was doing it, but I spent like twenty minutes just aligning them. 

And then with my ten-key—my calculator, which I use all day for auditing—I can't just type the numbers in normally right now. I have started tapping the calculator in sets of nine. Like, I'll just sit there tapping the plastic casing or the clear button, exactly nine times. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine. Over and over before I can actually do any of the math. It’s so distracting and it takes up so much time. 

But I think the part that really freaked out my coworker, and the reason I finally made this appointment, is the copier. I’ll go over to the machine to scan the ledgers or whatever, and I’ll just stop. I’ll stand there by the copier with my hands held up in the air, almost like I'm waiting to catch a basketball or like I'm just totally frozen, and I will literally just stand there holding my hands up until someone walks by and asks if I am okay. And as soon as they ask, I just put my hands down and snap out of it like nothing happened. I just don't know why my body is doing these things, but it's really starting to get in the way of everything.

But with this, it's not like that at all. There’s absolutely no warning. No tension in my muscles, no weird tingle in my fingers before I start tapping the ten-key, no... no pressure building up in my chest or my arms before I just freeze with my hands up at the copier. \n\nIt just happens. Like, just yesterday, I was sitting at my desk, and I had this huge stack of reconciliation forms—the ones for the third quarter that are always a complete nightmare because the sales team literally never categorizes their travel expenses right, they just dump it all under miscellaneous—and I was just looking at my dual monitors, totally relaxed, just trying to figure out if a hotel receipt was supposed to be lodging or client entertainment, and then... boom. Next thing I know, my hand is just tapping the plastic. One, two, three, four... all the way to nine. \n\nI didn't feel anything right before it started. I couldn't have held it back because I didn't even know it was about to happen until it was already happening. It's just like someone flips a switch and my body just does the movement without asking my permission or giving me any kind of heads-up, you know? It's completely spontaneous. So, yeah, no buildup or urge at all. It's just... sudden.\n\nDoctor: When you freeze with your hands up, if someone moves your arms into a different position, do they tend to stay there?\n\nPatient: Well, honestly, nobody has really tried to move my arms when I do that, so I'm not entirely sure if they would just stay there. Usually, people are just too weirded out to actually touch me. Like, my coworker Sarah—she sits in the cubicle right next to the copier, the one with all the little succulent plants on her desk—she’s usually the one who notices. She’ll just kind of peek over her monitor and say, \"Hey, are you okay?\" and the second she says it, I just drop my arms and snap out of it. \n\nBut, you know, I guess I should probably reiterate, because it's just so bizarre and it's the whole reason I'm even here talking to you right now... it's not just the freezing at the copier with my hands up in the air. It's all these things I've started doing at work, and even at school, that just completely do not make sense. Like I mentioned before, the other day I took that massive stack of receipts—these were for the petty cash box, which is always a total mess anyway—and instead of just logging them into the spreadsheet like I'm supposed to, I literally spent twenty minutes lining them up in this perfectly straight row all the way across the office floor. Just one after the other, end to end. \n\nAnd then there's the tapping the calculator in sets of nine, over and over, before I can even start auditing a ledger. It's just... I don't know, it's like my body is just doing these completely random, nonsensical things—the receipts on the floor, the tapping, the freezing with my hands up until someone checks on me—and it's really starting to disrupt my life. I just want to understand why I'm doing things that have absolutely no logic to them.\n\nDoctor: When these episodes happen, does it ever feel like an outside force is controlling your body?\n\nPatient: Um, no, not really like... I get this overwhelming feeling that they are messages directed entirely at me. \n\nLike last week, there was this invoice from our main office supply vendor, and the total was $412.18, and the due date was the 18th, and the account number ended in 412, and it just... it felt like someone, or some system, was trying to tell me something. Yeah, actually... yes. That happens a lot, especially lately, and it's honestly really frustrating because in my head, everything I'm saying makes perfect sense. But then I'll be talking, and I can just see the other person's face sort of... glaze over, or they'll look at me like I'm speaking a completely different language. 

Like, okay, for example, just the other day I was in Mr. Henderson's office again. I was trying to explain to him why one of the main operating ledgers was off by a couple hundred dollars. So I'm standing there, pointing at the spreadsheet on his monitor, and I start trying to explain the discrepancy. But as I'm talking, my brain just sort of... takes off on all these different tracks at once. 

I started out talking about why the ledger was off, but the dates on the missing entries reminded me of my own tuition deadlines for school—because I take some classes at the community college on the side, just trying to get my degree sorted out while I work—so I started talking about the tuition deadlines. And then, from there, my brain just immediately jumped to the new tax rules for educational deductions, because I had just read this huge article about how the tax rules were changing for student equipment. And that made me think about the studio lighting in this photography elective I'm taking, because the equipment costs for that class are ridiculous, and the wattage numbers on the studio lighting are so specific. And before I knew it, talking about the wattage numbers led me right back into talking about those number patterns I was telling you about earlier, the ones that feel like they're directed at me. 

So I'm just talking and talking, laying it all out, because to me, it's all completely linked together. It’s a straight line in my mind. But then Mr. Henderson just held up his hands and stopped me. He actually said, "I have absolutely no idea what you're talking about." And it's not just him—other people tell me that, too. They tell me they cannot follow how I got from one point to the next, like I'm skipping over all the bridges between my thoughts and just leaving them behind. They say I jump around so much that it just sounds like noise, which is awful, because I'm really just trying to explain the math. But I guess... yeah, I guess it just comes out all tangled up to everyone else.

It’s just a completely empty, physical thing.\n\nDoctor: Right before these movements happen, do you feel a buildup or urge in your body that you can hold back for a little while?\n\nPatient: Um, no, not really. I mean, I think I know what you mean, like... like when you have to sneeze, right? You feel that tickle in the back of your nose and you know it's coming, and maybe you can pinch your nose and stop it for a second if you really try. Or like an itch you can ignore for a minute. But with this, it's not like that at all. There’s absolutely no warning. No tension in my muscles, no weird tingle in my fingers before I start tapping the ten-key, no... no pressure building up in my chest or my arms before I just freeze with my hands up at the copier. \n\nIt just happens. Like, just yesterday, I was sitting at my desk, and I had this huge stack of reconciliation forms—the ones for the third quarter that are always a complete nightmare because the sales team literally never categorizes their travel expenses right, they just dump it all under miscellaneous—and I was just looking at my dual monitors, totally relaxed, just trying to figure out if a hotel receipt was supposed to be lodging or client entertainment, and then... boom. Next thing I know, my hand is just tapping the plastic. One, two, three, four... all the way to nine. \n\nI didn't feel anything right before it started. I couldn't have held it back because I didn't even know it was about to happen until it was already happening. It's just like someone flips a switch and my body just does the movement without asking my permission or giving me any kind of heads-up, you know? It's completely spontaneous. So, yeah, no buildup or urge at all. It's just... sudden.\n\nDoctor: When you freeze with your hands up, if someone moves your arms into a different position, do they tend to stay there?\n\nPatient: Well, honestly, nobody has really tried to move my arms when I do that, so I'm not entirely sure if they would just stay there. Usually, people are just too weirded out to actually touch me. Like, my coworker Sarah—she sits in the cubicle right next to the copier, the one with all the little succulent plants on her desk—she’s usually the one who notices. She’ll just kind of peek over her monitor and say, \"Hey, are you okay?\" and the second she says it, I just drop my arms and snap out of it. \n\nBut, you know, I guess I should probably reiterate, because it's just so bizarre and it's the whole reason I'm even here talking to you right now... it's not just the freezing at the copier with my hands up in the air. It's all these things I've started doing at work, and even at school, that just completely do not make sense. Like I mentioned before, the other day I took that massive stack of receipts—these were for the petty cash box, which is always a total mess anyway—and instead of just logging them into the spreadsheet like I'm supposed to, I literally spent twenty minutes lining them up in this perfectly straight row all the way across the office floor. Just one after the other, end to end. \n\nAnd then there's the tapping the calculator in sets of nine, over and over, before I can even start auditing a ledger. It's just... I don't know, it's like my body is just doing these completely random, nonsensical things—the receipts on the floor, the tapping, the freezing with my hands up until someone checks on me—and it's really starting to disrupt my life. I just want to understand why I'm doing things that have absolutely no logic to them.\n\nDoctor: When these episodes happen, does it ever feel like an outside force is controlling your body?\n\nPatient: Um, no, not really like... I don't feel like a puppet on strings or anything. It's not like an invisible hand is grabbing my wrist and forcing me to tap the calculator or line up the receipts on the floor. My body is doing it, even if I don't know why. But, you know, since you mention an outside force... there is something else that kind of feels like an outside presence is involved, just not physically controlling my muscles. \n\nIt's more about what I'm seeing when I'm working. And I know it sounds completely strange, I really do, and I've been kind of afraid to even bring it up because I know how it sounds, but... I get convinced that certain numbers at work are actually messages. Specifically about me. Like, I'll be doing the data entry for accounts payable—which I usually do on Tuesdays and Thursdays because that's when the big vendor batches come in from the mailroom—and I'll be looking at the screen, and suddenly I just *know* that certain invoice totals, specific client account numbers, and even the net-30 due dates aren't just random business data. I get this overwhelming feeling that they are messages directed entirely at me. \n\nLike last week, there was this invoice from our main office supply vendor, and the total was $412.18, and the due date was the 18th, and the account number ended in 412, and it just... it felt like someone, or some system, was trying to tell me something. I actually got so worked up about it that I took the physical paper invoice into my supervisor's office. His name is Mr. Henderson, and I usually hate interrupting him because he's always on these long conference calls with corporate, but I just had to show him. \n\nAnd he was really patient about it, honestly. I still feel like they are tracking me. Like whoever is sending these numbers is watching me through the system to see whether I understand the pattern they're laying out in the ledgers. So, it's not a force moving my hands, but it definitely feels like some outside force is communicating with me through the bookkeeping, if that makes any sense at all.\n\nDoctor: When you talk, do people often tell you that your speech is hard to follow or that you jump from one idea to another in a way that doesn’t make sense?\n\nPatient: Yeah, actually... yes. That happens a lot, especially lately, and it's honestly really frustrating because in my head, everything I'm saying makes perfect sense. And then, from there, my brain just immediately jumped to the new tax rules for educational deductions, because I had just read this huge article about how the tax rules were changing for student equipment. And that made me think about the studio lighting in this photography elective I'm taking, because the equipment costs for that class are ridiculous, and the wattage numbers on the studio lighting are so specific. It’s a straight line in my mind. But then Mr. Henderson just held up his hands and stopped me. He actually said, \"I have absolutely no idea what you're talking about.\" And it's not just him—other people tell me that, too. They tell me they cannot follow how I got from one point to the next, like I'm skipping over all the bridges between my thoughts and just leaving them behind. They say I jump around so much that it just sounds like noise, which is awful, because I'm really just trying to explain the math. But I guess... yeah, I guess it just comes out all tangled up to everyone else.\n\nDoctor: Do people ever tell you that your facial expression or emotional reactions seem odd or don’t match what’s going on?\n\nPatient: Um, well, it's not so much that they tell me my reactions are odd in a bizarre way, like I'm laughing when someone is crying or anything like that. It's more that they notice I don't really have much of a reaction at all anymore. Voices? Um... well, I mean... yes. But it's not like a whole crowd of people yelling or anything like that. It's usually just this one specific voice, and it only really happens when I'm completely by myself.

But... sometimes... \n\nI know it sounds strange, really strange, especially coming from someone who literally does bookkeeping for a living, but sometimes I get absolutely convinced that certain numbers are... well, they're not just data. Like, specific invoice totals, or the account numbers for certain vendors, or even the net-30 due dates on the accounts payable aging report... I start feeling like they are messages. About me. Specifically meant for me to find. \n\nLike, last Tuesday, I was reconciling the bank statement against our general ledger, and I noticed this sequence of invoice totals—$412.50, $41.25, and then an account number ending in 4125. And I just stopped. I sat there at my L-shaped desk, staring at my dual monitors, and my heart started racing because I just knew, I *knew*, it was a message. It felt like the system was trying to tell me something, or maybe test me. So I spent, like, three hours digging through old archived files, pulling up vendor histories from like three years ago, trying to trace the origin of the 4125 pattern, completely ignoring the rest of the daily deposits I was supposed to be working on. \n\nMy supervisor, Linda, she came over because she noticed I hadn't submitted the daily reconciliation report yet. She's usually really nice, she's been there for like fifteen years, and she sat down with me and looked at my screen. She pulled up the original invoices and the vendor contracts, and she walked me through it, step by step, showing me exactly why those totals were what they were. Like, one was just a standard order of printer toner with sales tax, and another was a prorated software license fee. She showed me all the documentation, proving they were just completely normal, everyday business entries. \n\nAnd logically, when she was explaining it, I could hear her words, and I could see the math on the screen. But even after she walked away, even after I finally submitted the report and went back to my turkey sandwich... I still felt it. Deep down. I still felt like those numbers were tracking me. Like whoever or whatever put them there was watching to see if I understood the pattern, to see if I was smart enough to figure out what the 4125 meant. And it's not just that one time, it happens with other numbers, too. It's like I can't shake the feeling that there's a hidden layer of meaning in the spreadsheets that only I am supposed to see, even when Linda proves to me that it's just regular accounting stuff. It's really hard to explain, but it just feels so real when it happens.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever feel that someone is watching you or trying to harm you?\n\nPatient: Watching me? Like, a person? No, no. I know I just said that thing about the numbers feeling like they were tracking me or testing me, which I guess sounds a little like being watched, but it's not a physical person spying on me or anything like that. And definitely no one is trying to harm me. \n\nMy L-shaped desk is tucked way in the back corner of the accounting floor, and my back is technically to the main walkway, which I guess would make some people paranoid, but I never feel like someone is standing behind me staring at the back of my head. I mean, the only people who even walk by are Dave, who is way too busy stressing out and clicking his retractable pen to care about what I'm doing, and Linda, and she's practically the nicest person in the world. She brings in glazed donuts every other Friday from this little bakery near her house. She's definitely not out to get me or sabotage my work. Nobody is trying to poison my turkey sandwich in the breakroom fridge or anything crazy like that. \n\nAnd outside of work, it's the same thing. Like when I'm walking to my car after my night classes at the community college, it's usually pretty dark out by then, especially in the winter, but I don't get spooked. I just walk straight to my car, get in, and drive home. I don't ever look in my rearview mirror and feel like there's someone following my car, and I don't think anyone is hiding in the bushes waiting to jump out at me. I don't feel in danger at all. I'm just a twenty-two-year-old bookkeeping clerk, you know? I don't think I'm important enough for anyone to want to follow me around or hurt me. It's really just that weird hidden-message feeling I get with the spreadsheets sometimes, but not actual people out to get me.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever hear voices when no one else is around?\n\nPatient: Voices? Um... well, I mean... yes. But it's not like a whole crowd of people yelling or anything like that. It's usually just this one specific voice, and it only really happens when I'm completely by myself. \n\nLike, I'll be sitting at my desk—that L-shaped one I was telling you about, tucked away in the back corner of the accounting floor. It gets really quiet back there, especially around four-thirty when Dave is off getting his afternoon coffee and Linda is wrapping up her daily emails. I'll just be sitting there, staring at my dual monitors, maybe scrolling through a massive Excel spreadsheet for the month-end reconciliation, and out of nowhere, I'll hear this man's voice. And it sounds so incredibly real, like someone is leaning right over my shoulder. He'll say something really specific, like, \"check line seven.\" \n\nAnd I mean, it's so clear and loud that I physically turn my office chair around. I'll spin around expecting to see Dave standing there holding his mug, or maybe a courier who wandered into the wrong department, but... there's literally no one. Just the empty carpeted walkway and the hum of the overhead air conditioner. I'll even stand up and look over the cubicle wall just to be absolutely sure, but I'm completely alone. \n\nAnd it's not just at work, either. It happens sometimes when I'm leaving my night classes at the community college, too. Like I said before, I usually just walk straight to my car, and it's pretty dark and empty out in that parking lot by the time my accounting ethics class gets out. Sometimes, when I'm halfway across the asphalt, just me and the orange streetlights, I'll hear that exact same man's voice. He'll say something like, \"you missed the sign.\" \n\nI'll stop dead in my tracks right there in the cold. I'll look all around, checking behind the parked cars, looking back toward the brick wall of the science building, because I swear to you, it sounds like a real person is walking two steps behind me. But the lot is totally empty. And then I just stand there overthinking it, wondering, what sign? Did I miss a literal parking sign, or does he mean a sign like the weird number patterns at work? It really messes with my head because the voice doesn't feel like a thought inside my brain, you know? It sounds like it's traveling through the air, hitting my eardrums exactly the way your voice is right now. I've even pulled my phone out of my jacket pocket to see if maybe a YouTube video started playing by accident, or if I pocket-dialed a podcast, but my screen is always black. It's just... it's just this guy's voice speaking right to me, and I have absolutely no idea where it's coming from."
